units.t: Mythology. Episode four.
In this episode: Egypt's gods and the journey after death, The Aztec gods and the Fifth Sun and The orishas: Yoruba gods of two continents.
Part one. Egypt's gods and the journey after death.
For well over a thousand years, Egyptians believed your heart would be weighed against a feather when you died.
What happened next depended on how you'd lived.
A religion that lasted millennia.
Ancient Egyptian religion was not one fixed system.
Over roughly 3,000 years it included hundreds of gods, many tied to particular towns, whose roles shifted and merged.
The sun god Ra, for example, was later combined with Amun of Thebes as Amun-Ra.
Gods were often shown with animal heads to signal their qualities: jackal-headed Anubis watched over the dead, and ibis-headed Thoth was god of writing and wisdom.
Our sources include the Pyramid Texts, carved inside royal pyramids from around 2400 BC and among the oldest religious writings known, plus later coffin inscriptions, papyri and temple walls.
Ra and the first land.
Egyptian creation stories begin with Nun, dark, endless waters.
From them rose a mound of land, just as fields emerged each year when the Nile flood went down.
In a version from Heliopolis, the creator god Atum produced Shu, air, and Tefnut, moisture, whose children were Geb, earth, and Nut, sky.
The sun god Ra was central to daily life.
By day he sailed across the sky in a boat.
By night he journeyed through the underworld, fighting the chaos serpent Apep, to be reborn each dawn.
Pharaohs called themselves the 'son of Ra'.
Osiris, Set, Isis and Horus.
The most important Egyptian myth concerns Osiris, a wise king who taught people farming and law.
His brother Set, god of storms, deserts and disorder, was jealous.

The Greek writer Plutarch, around AD 100, gives the fullest telling: Set tricked Osiris into a beautifully made chest, slammed the lid and threw it into the Nile, then cut the body up and scattered it.
Isis, Osiris's wife and sister, searched Egypt for the pieces and, with Nephthys and Anubis, put him back together, in effect making the first mummy.
Osiris became ruler of the dead.
Their son Horus, raised in hiding in the Nile Delta marshes, fought Set for the throne and lost an eye, which was restored.
The Eye of Horus became a popular protective amulet, and each living pharaoh was identified with Horus.
What makes a person.
Egyptians saw a person as made of several parts.
The ka was the life force, which needed food and drink offerings even after death.
The ba, often shown as a bird with a human head, could move between the tomb and the world.
Your name and your shadow mattered too.
For these to survive, the body had to be preserved.
The goal was to become an akh, a transfigured spirit, and reach the Field of Reeds, an ideal version of Egypt with perfect harvests.
Small servant figures called shabtis were buried with the dead to do farm work for them there.
Weighing the heart.
The dead faced judgement in the Hall of Two Truths, pictured in the Book of the Dead.
The deceased first declared the wrongs they had not committed.
Anubis then placed their heart on a scale against a feather representing Maat, goddess of truth, justice and cosmic order, while Thoth recorded the result.
A heart weighed down by wrongdoing was eaten by Ammit, part crocodile, part lion and part hippopotamus.
A balanced heart meant the person could join Osiris.
That is why mummification left the heart in place, with a heart scarab spell begging it not to testify against its owner.
The brain was discarded, as thinking was thought to happen in the heart.
A priest then performed the Opening of the Mouth, so the dead could breathe, eat and speak again.
The key idea: Ancient Egyptian religion lasted about 3,000 years, with hundreds of gods whose roles shifted and merged over time.
Part two. The Aztec gods and the Fifth Sun.
The Mexica believed they lived under the fifth sun the gods had made, and that it moved only because gods had given their lives.
Their religion was built around keeping it in the sky.
The Mexica and their city.
The name "Aztec" was popularised much later.
The builders of Tenochtitlan called themselves the Mexica, and their name lives on in Mexico.
In their own tradition, they migrated south from a homeland called Aztlan, guided by their patron god Huitzilopochtli.
He promised they would know their new home when they saw an eagle perched on a cactus growing from a rock.
They found that sign on a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, where they founded Tenochtitlan, traditionally in 1325.
The eagle on the cactus is now at the centre of Mexico's flag.
Within two centuries the island had become one of the largest cities in the world, linked to the shore by causeways.
Four suns and the Fifth.
In Mexica cosmology, time moved in great ages called Suns, each a separate creation that ended in catastrophe.
In one widely told version, the first world was destroyed by jaguars, the second by winds, the third by a rain of fire and the fourth by a flood.
Accounts differ, since our sources were written after the Spanish conquest.
The Fifth Sun, Nahui Ollin, was also destined to end, many believed, in earthquakes.
After the fourth world, the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan.
Proud Tecciztecatl lost his nerve four times; humble, sickly Nanahuatzin leapt into the fire and rose as the sun.
Ashamed, Tecciztecatl followed.
A god threw a rabbit into his face, dimming him into the moon.
Even then the sun would not move until the other gods gave their lives.
War, rain and rivals.
At the heart of Tenochtitlan stood the Templo Mayor, a stepped pyramid topped by two shrines.
One honoured Huitzilopochtli, the Mexica's patron god of the sun and war.
The other honoured Tlaloc, an ancient god of rain and fertility.
Together they represented war and agriculture, the twin foundations of the empire.
Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed, defeated his siblings who plotted against his mother Coatlicue, and cast his dismembered sister Coyolxauhqui down the hill.
Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent, was linked with wind, learning and the morning star.
His rival Tezcatlipoca, the "Smoking Mirror", was a powerful god of night, fate and sorcery.
In one cycle of tales they alternately create and destroy the earlier Suns.
Debt and sacrifice.
Mexica sacrifice followed from their myths.
The gods gave their lives to create and power the Fifth Sun, so humans owed a debt that had to be repaid.
Worshippers offered incense, food, flowers and their own blood, drawn with cactus spines or bone points.
Most dramatically, priests sacrificed human beings, many of them war captives, at ceremonies across the ritual year.
Spanish accounts of the scale were sometimes exaggerated, and historians long debated them, but archaeology has confirmed that sacrifice was real and significant.
Since 2015, excavations in Mexico City have uncovered parts of the Huei Tzompantli, a great rack and tower built with the skulls of hundreds of individuals, near the Templo Mayor.
Myths after the conquest.
Hernán Cortés conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521, with tens of thousands of Indigenous allies.
A famous story claims the emperor Moctezuma believed Cortés was the returning Quetzalcoatl.
Many historians now doubt this, since it appears mainly in sources written decades after the conquest, shaped by Spanish and Indigenous writers trying to explain what had happened.
One tale has Quetzalcoatl departing east, promising in some versions to return.
The Mexica religion was suppressed, its temples demolished and a cathedral built near the ruins.
Yet much survived.
In 1978 electricity workers in Mexico City uncovered a huge carved stone of the dismembered Coyolxauhqui, leading to the full excavation of the Templo Mayor.
More than a million and a half people in Mexico still speak Nahuatl, the Mexica language.
The key idea: The people we call the Aztecs called themselves the Mexica and founded Tenochtitlan on a lake island.
Part three. The orishas: Yoruba gods of two continents.
From the cities of south-western Nigeria to the beaches of Brazil and the streets of Havana, millions of people honour the orishas, divine forces of thunder, rivers, iron and the sea.
The Yoruba world.
The Yoruba are one of Africa's largest ethnic groups, numbering tens of millions, mostly in south-western Nigeria and neighbouring Benin and Togo.
Their traditional religion, Ìṣẹ̀ṣe, recognises a supreme creator, Olodumare, who is vast and distant and not usually approached directly.
Instead, people relate to the orishas, divine beings who act as intermediaries and govern particular forces of nature and areas of life.
Some are seen as forces present since creation, others as deified ancestors and kings.
There is also àṣẹ, the vital power that makes things happen, flowing through gods, people, words and objects.
Today many Yoruba are Christian or Muslim, but traditional practice and its influence remain strong.
Land from water.
One widely told creation story begins with the world as water and marsh.
Olodumare sends the orisha Obatala down from the sky on a golden chain, carrying a snail shell full of earth and a bird, often described as a hen or cockerel.
Obatala pours out the earth, and the bird scratches and scatters it, spreading dry land.
In some versions Obatala becomes drunk on palm wine and falls asleep, and his rival Oduduwa completes the task.
Obatala is also said to shape human bodies from clay, and some traditions explain disabilities as the result of his drunkenness.
His followers therefore avoid palm wine and protect people with disabilities.
The place where land first appeared is Ile-Ife, still regarded as sacred.
A pantheon of personalities.
The orishas are vivid personalities.
Obatala, associated with white cloth and coolness, stands for purity, wisdom and calm judgement.
Ogun, orisha of iron, tools and war, is honoured by blacksmiths, hunters and, today, drivers and mechanics.
Shango, lord of thunder and lightning, is remembered as a fiery king of Oyo, and his symbol is a double-headed axe.
Oshun, orisha of sweet waters, love, beauty and fertility, is linked with the Osun River, and her sacred grove at Osogbo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Yemoja is a great mother associated with water.
Eshu, or Elegba, the trickster messenger, guards crossroads, carries offerings, and must be honoured first in many ceremonies.
Ifá: reading destiny.
Facing a serious decision, illness or trouble, a person may consult a babalawo, a priest of Ifá.
Ifá is linked with Orunmila, the orisha of wisdom and destiny.
The babalawo casts a divining chain, or manipulates sacred palm nuts, to produce one of 256 possible patterns called odu.
Each odu is associated with a large collection of memorised verses, stories and proverbs.
The priest recites them, and priest and client together interpret which passage speaks to the situation, often followed by recommended offerings.
Training takes many years.
UNESCO has recognised Ifá divination as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and its verses are treasured as a vast store of Yoruba history, values and wisdom.
Across the Atlantic.
During the Atlantic slave trade, especially in its final decades, large numbers of Yoruba people were taken to the Americas, particularly Cuba and Brazil.
Pressured to become Catholic, many kept the orishas alive in secret.
Each orisha came to be linked with a Catholic saint of similar imagery: Shango with St Barbara, whose symbols include lightning, and Oshun with Cuba's Virgin of Charity.
Scholars debate how far this was disguise and how far blending.
From this grew Santería, Lucumí, in Cuba and Candomblé in Brazil, with drumming, dance, possession and initiation.
Yemoja became Yemayá in Cuba and Iemanjá in Brazil, queen of the sea.
On 2 February crowds in Salvador carry gifts to the sea for her, and many Brazilians toss flowers into the waves on New Year's Eve.
The key idea: Yoruba religion centres on a distant creator and the orishas, divine forces who govern nature and life.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What best describes ancient Egyptian religion?
Answer. Hundreds of gods whose roles shifted.
Question two. According to Mexica tradition, how did they choose where to found their city?
Answer. Their god promised a sign to guide them.
Question three. How do Yoruba people usually relate to the creator Olodumare?
Answer. Through the orishas as intermediaries.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
